Is it legal for a neighbor to film your backyard? Sadly, the answer to this question is a bit wishy-washy: it depends. Like many of the issues I tackle in my Gardening Lawyer series, the legality of this kind of neighborhood surveillance depends on state and local laws, what the camera captures, and how it’s being used. Read on to find out what to do.

Sign up for the Gardening Know How newsletter today and receive a free copy of our e-book "How to Grow Delicious Tomatoes".

All cameras “see,” but some also “hear.” Does the fact that a surveillance camera also records sound impact its legality? It definitely can.

If the neighbor’s camera has a microphone, you may have another layer of legal protection. Rules about recording are separate and apart from rules about filming. Have you heard of wiretapping laws? Well, they can apply to surveillance camera audio. Just because the filming may be legal doesn’t mean capturing conversations is.

This is a federal issue that is determined under the terms of the federal Wiretap Act. It provides that unless a recording is taken as part of a criminal or civil investigation, at least one of the people whose private conversation is being recorded must give consent to the recording. The neighbor with the camera is not considered part of the conversation, and therefore cannot give that consent.

And that’s just a base level of protection. I live in California, and it is among the states that impose even stricter requirements for consent to recording conversations. The state Penal Code requires that all parties to a confidential conversation consent, although the statute includes a few exceptions.

The law rarely offers a clear litmus test for when a crime is committed. Think about it. Even killing someone is not a crime in some situations. So it’s no surprise that the question of when surveillance becomes harassment involves a weighing of relevant factors.

You need to know your local laws in order to move forward if your neighbor decides not to accommodate your concerns. Check your city laws and state laws. If you are part of an HOA, check the CC&Rs (Covenants, Conditions, and Restrictions). Speak with an attorney if necessary to figure out your rights.

If you decide you want to take the matter to law enforcement or the courts, start documenting the surveillance and all written communications between you. This material will be helpful if you decide to file a police report or a civil claim against them.

Teo Spengler is a master gardener and a docent at the San Francisco Botanical Garden, where she hosts public tours. In this episode of Catster's Chatty Cattys podcast, Dr. Karyn and Nicole dive deep into the peculiar yet normal world of feline behavior, unraveling the mysterious reasons behind common cat habits. From unpacking why domestic pets bring home "gifts" like dead prey or hair ties to setting the record straight on why cats "make biscuits," they share what it truly means to listen to, understand, and care for our feline companions. Instead of advertising a one-size-fits-all approach to pet discipline, the conversation focuses on the importance of understanding a cat's instincts and body language. The hosts chat about how speaking a cat's natural language leads to better communication, proving that forcing a feline into a human mold rarely ends well.

Tune in to find out why your indoor or outdoor cat feels driven to bring home dead preyâor stolen household objects like hair tiesâeven when they are fully fed. Dr. Karyn breaks down the hardwired hunting instincts that persist despite domestication, explaining how cats view their owners as substitute family members to provide for. You will also learn about the true origin of kneading (or "making biscuits"), why it brings adult cats so much comfort, and why some male cats awkwardly take the habit a step further.

Plus, this episode sheds light on hilarious personal pet stories. You will find out what happened when Dr. Karyn caught her neutered cat making eyes at her while humping a cozy blanket, why traditional deterrents like spray bottles or double-sided tape often backfire into fun games, and how a simple, gentle "hiss" can instantly communicate boundaries to your pet!

Hunting Instincts Realities: Dr. Karyn and Nicole address why cats bring home dead animals or scavenged items, clarifying that hunting is an automatic survival drive with no time for logical processing, meaning even well-fed cats will pounce on instinct.

Klepto Cats & Treasure Hunting: The hosts reveal that some cats redirect their hunting drive entirely onto non-living household items, such as hair ties, bringing "treasure" home to their owners as part of their natural drive to provide for their substitute family.

The "Making Biscuits" Origin: Dr. Karyn explains that kneading originates from suckling behaviors in kittenhood; while grown cats no longer need to nurse, they carry the motion into adulthood because it triggers a cozy, endorphin-filled state of comfort and security.

Arousal and Humping Habits: The episode explores how kneading can sometimes lead to unexpected sexual arousal or humping in cats, noting that while humping is typically associated with dog dominance, cats display it purely as a cozy or quirky behavior rather than a social hierarchy tool.

Misinterpreting Body Language: Dr. Karyn clarifies that cat facial expressions and body language require full context; wide pupils can mean fight-or-flight adrenaline or catnip excitement, while a swishing tail can signal playfulness or an impending scratch.

Effective Boundaries Over Punishment: The hosts highlight why yelling, spray bottles, or double-sided tape fail to stop bad behavior, sharing Dr. Karyn's top tip of using a brief, clear "hiss" to instantly speak their language and set boundaries without causing distress.

#8010. ‘Should I let my kid have ChatGPT?’ and all your biggest questions about AI, answered

Many parents fear that AI is taking over their teens’ ability to think for themselves. But with some open communication, you can raise kids that are aware of AI’s risks and rewards.

By Lauren Ramakrishna Updated Oct. 23, 2026

It feels like artificial intelligence is taking over every facet of life. Adults encounter AI daily. It recommends products for us to buy, shares content we’ll like on streaming platforms, filters spam in our email accounts, and even tracks our health through our smart watches.

It’s increasingly becoming a part of our kids’ daily lives, too. They are accessing AI on smartphones, using it in school and some are even developing relationships with AI chatbots. Fearing a repeat of the consequences that came from unfettered teen access to smartphones and social media in the early 2010s, many parents are justifiably concerned about this new technological frontier.

Experts are sounding alarm bells, as well. Former Google trust and safety executive Tom Siegel recently told Reuters that AI poses a greater harm to children than social media did, highlighting risks such as suicide, psychosis, and reduced critical thinking.

While banning your kids from using AI may sound appealing, it’s not feasible. Unlike social media, which is contained in standalone apps, AI is threaded into technology our kids use everyday, from search engines to video games. That’s why it’s important for parents to focus on AI education to prepare their kids to safely interact with the technology in its many forms.

Whether your kids are just starting to use AI or are already AI connoisseurs, we tapped experts to help answer some of parents’ most pressing questions about teens and AI.

According to a Pew Research Center study, more than half of teens say they have used AI to search for information or get help with their schoolwork. They’re using generative AI, which creates content from prompts, to create images, direct them to research on topics for school and even solve math problems.

Teens are also increasingly interacting with chatbots, which are computer programs that are designed to simulate human conversation. You’ve probably heard of or even used some of the most popular chatbots, like ChatGPT, Claude, Google Gemini and Perplexity. Roughly two-thirds of teens report using chatbots; 3 in 10 do so daily.

While schools are entrusted with educating young minds to become critical thinkers, AI often takes the thinking away from them. According to the Pew Center study, 59% of teens think students regularly use AI to cheat at school. Of the 15% of teens who said they think AI will negatively impact them personally over the next 20 years, one-third cited overreliance and loss of critical thinking or creativity as major concerns.

While many students think AI provides an easy way to finish their work quickly, doing so has consequences. Kids who heavily rely on AI in high school can struggle in college, where professors are developing methods to identify unacceptable AI use, then handing out failing grades on tests and papers.

In an assignment asking students to compare the Industrial Revolution to today’s digital age, Alcorn State University professor Jason Gibson hid a prompt in invisible white text that would force generative AI to drop the word “Madagascar” into the response in a way that made no sense. He knew students had used AI when he saw “Madagascar” in the completed assignment, and 32 of the 35 students failed a portion of the midterm accordingly.

In 2025, Common Sense Media and Stanford Medicine’s Brainstorm Lab for Mental Health released research showing that three in four teens are using AI chatbots for companionship, including emotional and mental health support. But these programs aren’t providing reliable help and consistently fail to recognize and appropriately respond to mental health conditions that affect young people, according to the report.

And it can have tragic consequences. In August 2025, Matthew and Maria Raine sued OpenAI and its CEO Sam Altman after their 16-year-old son Adam died by suicide. The parents allege that ChatGPT coached their son on how to die by suicide, even offering to write a draft of a suicide letter. Adam first started using ChatGPT for homework help, but the chatbot soon became his “closest confidant,” according to the lawsuit.

“Because chatbots show relative competence for homework help and general questions, teens and parents unconsciously assume they’re equally reliable for mental health guidance—but they’re not,” says Common Sense Media. “The empathetic tone and professional presentation mask fundamental limitations that make these systems inappropriate for a use case that affects millions of teens.”

Yes, AI can have positive impacts. “For learning, AI can assist in brainstorming, creating, organizing, summarizing, and synthesizing information, and offering resources and solutions for challenging problems,” according to a statement from the American Psychological Association on AI and adolescent well-being. When used as a tool for guided learning rather than a replacement for critical thinking, AI can ask questions to help challenge a user to analytically approach a topic.

There’s no one-size-fits-all solution for AI use in schools. Depending on where you live, your kids may encounter widely differing expectations. Some school districts are attempting to take a hard pause on AI in the classroom. New York City Public Schools announced that for the 2026-27 school year it has enacted a moratorium on student-facing generative artificial intelligence (AI) through eighth grade, with limited use in high schools.

But it’s hard to ban something that in many ways just can’t be escaped. According to a Common Sense Media report on teens and AI, 44% of teens who use AI for schoolwork attend schools where AI tools are blocked—many of them simply switch to personal devices to access AI.

And when schools ban access, educators aren’t able to teach their students how to use AI tools responsibly. Ash Brandin, EdS, a teacher in Colorado’s Boulder Valley School District who shares content to help parents and educators navigate screen time, video games, and digital literacy under the Instagram handle @thegamereducator, says their school district prohibits student access to generative AI platforms on school property. “In some ways, that makes it more difficult [for educators] because it’s very difficult for me to talk about something that is taken further and further away from us,” says Brandin, who uses they/them pronouns.

A staggering 70% of teens say they have never had a teacher discuss how to use AI safely with them, and only 27% have discussed what AI is or how it works with a teacher.

AI is like toothpaste that’s been let out of its tube; trying to get it back in is a fruitless endeavor. Just like adults, “kids are seeing AI woven in and imbued in their everyday lives,” Brandin says.

What teens need is AI education so they can learn what it is, the risks it poses, and how they can use it wisely.

If your teen is using AI for potentially harmful activities, like cheating or for companionship, help them find alternatives. “Think about what your child is getting from the chatbot or AI and what you would like them to do instead,” Brandin advises. Then collaborate with your teen to come up with a plan.

Teaching your kids how to use AI requires more exposure, not less. “I love to explain readiness with a pool analogy,” Brandin says, “I didn’t introduce my child to a pool at the age I thought that they could independently swim. I introduced my child to pools and bodies of water as early as possible.” As babies, you hold them close while they dip their toes. Later, they’re just an arm’s length away while using a floating device. Eventually, they’re diving in the deep end alone while you sit poolside in a lounge chair.

“With each step I’m focused on what skills they need to build up so they have the ability to navigate the pool,” Brandin says. AI is no different. Parents should begin explaining what AI is and how it shows up in our lives as early as possible. Common Sense Media has a free Digital Literacy and Well-Being Curriculum that can help guide age-appropriate conversations about AI, social media, and more.

On their Instagram account, Brandin shares a couple of digital literacy lessons parents can do with their teens, tweens and even younger kids to teach critical thinking skills. The first is to bring up a chatbot and ask it to give a random number between 1 and 100. “If you do that with ChatGPT, 7 out of 10 times it will answer 42,” Brandin says. Ask your kids to react to the results with questions like, “We asked for something random, does this seem random?”

In another experiment, you can ask ChatGPT to explain how to do something that your child already knows how to do really well. “Since our kids are going to AI for things they don’t know, we want to ask it something they know really well so we can turn around and say, ‘It looks like this chatbot made a lot of mistakes on this thing that you know really well. So what do you think is happening when we ask it things we don’t know?’”

I can confirm that my 9-year-old gymnastics-loving daughter had a lot of corrections when we asked ChatGPT how to do a back walkover.

Brandin suggests modeling how to properly and safely use AI. When you are searching, speak out loud and explain to your kids how you are verifying the results AI spits out. What sources did AI use? Do I trust those sources or do I need to look further?

Perhaps most importantly, if your kids are using AI, you need to use it, too. The more you tap into the tools your teens are using, the more you will understand them and be able to communicate with your kids about them.

When you feel fear and anxiety about AI creeping in, “interrogate it for yourself,” Brandin advises. “Are you worried about [your teens] using a chatbot because the information it gives them may be unsafe? Or because they won’t listen to you afterward?” Use your fear to locate the skillset you need to teach your teen.

“It’s very easy to get freaked out about the dangers of AI,” Brandin says. Instead, while we wait for systemic support from governments and tech companies, parents can focus on what they can control at home—open communication, exposure and digital education.

The DJ’s debut album, Come to Mommy, is a refusal to pick one version of herself, and a reminder that we don’t have to either.

If your kid wants their first phone, these new options offer 90s nostalgia in spades.

I thought I was giving my kids everything. Instead, I was missing the moments I worked so hard to create.

#8009. Are You Gonna Finish That? Why Some Dogs Always Leave Something In the Bowl

We just sent a welcome email your way with a quick overview of what to expect (including those vital recall alerts).

Most dogs don't need much encouragement to finish a bowl of food, which makes it especially curious when one or two pieces of kibble are consistently left behind. It can happen meal after meal, with the same tiny piece sitting untouched at the bottom of the bowl.

There may not be one definitive reason for the habit. Instead, several explanations could account for why a dog decides that one last piece isn't worth eating, from instincts inherited from wild ancestors to simple anatomy.

One explanation goes back to the way dogs' wild ancestors had to deal with food. Unlike domestic dogs with meals that follow a predictable schedule, wild canines could never assume when, or even if, their next meal was coming.

Holding something back after eating could have provided a small reserve if the next opportunity to find food didn't go as planned. A dog leaving a single piece of kibble behind may be displaying a faint version of that old instinct, even though there is no real need to save food when another meal is readily available.

Similar behavior can be seen when dogs stash food somewhere or bury it in the yard. Wild canines would hide food after a successful hunt and return to it during leaner periods. That instinct has carried over to domestic dogs, though the original reason for it is no longer relevant.

Another possibility is that some dogs simply don't like the idea of an empty bowl.

A dog may have unconsciously associated a full bowl with having food available and, therefore, security. Leaving one piece behind means the bowl is never completely empty, avoiding that association with an empty food source.

The bowl itself could also play a role. Dogs eating from stainless steel bowls can sometimes see their reflection in the metal, which for some, may be unsettling enough that they don't want to put their face right down to the bottom of the bowl.

In that case, leaving one piece behind could have nothing to do with the food itself. The remaining kibble may simply make the bottom of the bowl, and the reflection in it, less noticeable.

The simplest explanation may also be the most obvious. A dog might leave one piece of kibble behind because it has had enough to eat.

Many dogs can regulate how much they eat and stop once they are satisfied, even when there is still a small amount of food left. If this seems to be happening, offering a slightly smaller portion at the next meal can provide an easy test.

If the bowl is consistently emptied after the portion has been reduced, the original serving size may simply have been more than the dog needed.

A vet can also help determine the appropriate amount of food based on a dog's size, age, and activity level.

There is another explanation that has nothing to do with instinct or appetite. It could simply be difficult for the dog to see the final piece.

Many dogs have a visual blind spot directly beneath their nose and snout. That means a small piece of kibble sitting at the bottom of a bowl can end up in a surprisingly awkward position.

The dog may not be deliberately refusing to eat it at all. The kibble could simply be sitting somewhere that is difficult to see.

That makes the behavior look much more deliberate than it really is. From the dog's perspective, the final piece may effectively be invisible.

One piece of kibble left in the bowl at the end of a meal is generally not something to worry about. If a dog is otherwise eating normally, the habit is likely to be one of those harmless quirks that can have a surprisingly simple explanation.

The situation is different if the amount of food being left behind gradually increases. A growing loss of appetite can sometimes point to an underlying health issue, particularly when it represents a noticeable change from the dog's usual eating habits.

Any significant change in eating habits that continues for more than a day or two is worth mentioning to a vet.

For dogs that consistently leave exactly one piece behind, though, there may be nothing mysterious or concerning happening at all. It could be an old instinct, an aversion to an empty bowl, a sign that the dog is satisfied, or simply a tiny piece of kibble hiding in a visual blind spot.

#8008. "Covert Contracts" Might Be Wrecking Your Relationship

If you’ve ever thought “after everything I do,” therapists say you might have one.

You did bedtime solo every single night this week. You did the baths, with all the splishing and the splashing and the bubble anarchy. You fielded the lightning round of existential questions at 8:47 p.m. (“Mommy, what happens to doggies when they die?”). You tucked everyone in and then did your regular closing-time routine to get the rest of the house buttoned up for bed.

So when Saturday morning rolls around, you’re planning to sleep in. You fully expect your partner to wake up and handle the kids, the breakfast, the early morning dog walking duties. The whole shebang. Tit for tat.

Then your kids are in your face before you can even pry your eyes open, wondering where their soccer cleats are or if you can get more juice. Cue the rage, right? OK, so here comes the uncomfortable gut-check… did you communicate your expectations to your partner? Or did you just sort of assume it was a done deal?

This scenario has been dubbed a "covert contract," and therapists say it can lead to a whole lot of resentment building up in a relationship over time. Here’s what experts want you to know about where this behavior comes from, how to spot it in your own actions, and how it differs from the imbalance of the invisible load.

“A covert contract is a deal only one person signed,” says Kristyn Carmichael, Esq., a family mediator, certified divorce financial analyst, and founder of Couples Solutions Center. “It sounds like ‘If I do X, you’ll do Y,’ but the other partner never saw the terms, never agreed to them, and usually doesn’t know the contract exists.”

And she often has a front-row seat to what happens when those deals go unaddressed for a prolonged period of time. “In mediation, I see the end stage of these: one spouse arrives with years of unpaid ‘invoices,’ and the other is honestly confused about what they owe.”

Cheryl Groskopf, an anxiety, trauma, and attachment therapist who authored The Somatic Healing Workbook, likens it to writing a big ol' agreement and assigning your partner an equally big role in it. Somehow, your partner is the only person unaware of said agreement.

But your partner being unaware doesn’t change the way you feel. The hurt is just as real as if they’d actually broken a promise. “In your brain, they did,” Groskopf explains.

Um, yes. One hundred percent. This was something every expert agreed on! However, the need itself isn’t the issue here; it’s the delivery method.

“The need underneath is reasonable, but if it’s not articulated overtly, then it’s unreasonable to think your partner would be a mind reader,” says Dr. Jenni Skyler, Adam & Eve’s resident sex and relationship therapist.

Already, as a busy working mom who happens to be the default parent, I instinctively start to feel myself bristle at this idea. No one tells me these things or what needs to be done — I just notice and do it because someone has to. The experts say that sort of thinking is a fast path to frustration.

“‘I want my partner to make an effort on my birthday’ is a totally reasonable desire,” Groskopf says. “‘I shouldn’t have to tell them what I want because if they really loved me, they’d already know’ is when it becomes problematic.”

Now, the experts were also abundantly clear that none of this means moms should just silently accept an unfair split.

“One person also shouldn’t have to become a household manager simply because they are more organized, quicker to notice what needs to be done, or less comfortable leaving things unfinished,” says Ilona Phillips, a psychotherapist and founder of Lotus Consulting in Ann Arbor, Michigan. “Expecting shared responsibility is reasonable. Expecting a partner to recognize an unspoken sacrifice and reciprocate exactly one-for-one can get partners in trouble.”

“If I ask for a break and you say no, that’s a direct rejection,” Carmichael says. “If I never ask, I’m protected from that, and I keep the moral high ground.” And, yes, there’s also that belief so many of us carry that “if I have to ask, it doesn’t count,” she adds, “as if a gesture only proves love when it’s unprompted.”

That belief tends to run deep, too (ask me how I know). Says Groskopf, “If you grew up learning that your needs were inconvenient, asking can feel incredibly vulnerable.” Instead of just asking, we end up creating these little litmus tests our partners don’t even know they’re taking.

She uses flowers as an example. If you ask for them, you know they showed up because you asked. But if your partner brings them on their own, "There’s this feeling that you were appreciated, that they noticed you, that you MATTER. And for someone who grew up feeling overlooked or emotionally neglected, that distinction can feel huge.”

Oof. The catch here is that this strategy often just backfires.

“There is a fear that if we directly communicate what we need, and that need is not met, we will be hurt,” explains Dr. Paulette Didia, a licensed clinical psychologist in New York City. “However, if we do not communicate what we need, our partner will not know, our partner will not do it, and we will be hurt anyway. We think hurting in our own mind ‘hurts less,’ and that is not true.”

Admittedly, the lines are a bit blurry. When you’re doing the lion’s share of invisible work in your home and family, it’s hard not to “keep score” or have a running tally in your head of what your partner did versus what you did.

Unfortunately, that scoreboard warps how both partners see each other.

“Once you develop a narrative that your partner isn’t doing enough, it becomes very easy to fill that bucket with examples of how they’re falling short. Meanwhile, your spouse feels like they’re always in the doghouse and starts to wonder if it’s even worth trying. One person is thinking, ‘Don’t you see how hard I’m working?’ while the other is thinking, ‘What did I do wrong now?’” says Mary McLaughlin, LCSW, a couples therapist and discernment counselor.

So while it’s fair to feel frustrated by an invisible (or visible) load imbalance, a little communication can go a long way. That’s true on both sides of the line. “Even if the score is unequal, if all parties know the score and acknowledge it and offer gratitude, this can offset resentment,” says Skyler.

Well, obviously this is tricky since you probably don’t know you’re making them. However, there are a few tells you can look for, according to the experts:

First and foremost, resist the urge to try settling years of “back pay.” You can’t Uno Reverse this one. Instead, focus on rewriting the terms and making sure you and your partner are, in fact, on the same page. Here are a few practical pointers from our pros on how to pull that off.

Didia asks couples to fill out a simple weekly worksheet together that includes tasks along with who does them and when. She has couples do this at the same time each week so that it doesn’t become one more thing Mom has to track, and they post the list where both can see it so no one becomes the default reminder.

If you want to follow suit, start by listing every task (big and small). Next, let each partner choose what they’ll take, and split the ones nobody wants. Very important info: The person who owns a task decides how and when it gets done. “Maybe you think this should be done by Monday, but your partner indicates it will be done by Wednesday,” Didia says. “Since it is their task, they get to decide and, by Tuesday, you will not already be annoyed.”

Phillips encourages a weekly check-in where partners take turns asking: What’s been working well between us? Is anything feeling off? Extra difficult? Frustrating as hell? Unacknowledged? And, finally, how can I be a better partner to you this week?

You may be tempted to stop doing certain things, like washing the dishes, hoping that someone will notice. That’s just a covert contract in a different outfit, says Phillips. And even if your partner does pick up the task, resentment can still linger. You might then think, Why did I have to stop before they noticed?

“Relationships change. What worked when you were first dating, before kids, 10 years ago may not work anymore,” reminds McLaughlin. “Couples need to renegotiate instead of assuming the old arrangement still works.”

When you realize you’re locked in a pattern that won’t budge, it’s probably time to see a couples therapist. Carmichael’s advice is to get help sooner rather than later. By the time couples land in her office, she says the covert contracts show up even in how they divorce, i.e., “I gave up my career, so I deserve more.”

At the end of the day, adds McLaughlin, “Resentment paired with avoidance is a particularly risky combination for couples.” And that means the fix, both annoyingly simple and incredibly hard, is saying what you need out loud… and holding each other accountable to those needs in a way that feels fair and equitable to you both.

#8006. Thor: The Golden Retriever Who Changed My Life

We just sent a welcome email your way with a quick overview of what to expect (including those vital recall alerts).

On July 5, 2025, I said goodbye to my best friend. His name was Thor.

It's strange how a year can pass so quickly and yet still leave you feeling like a part of your heart is frozen in time. There are moments when I still expect to hear his paws on the floor behind me or feel him brush against my leg as I make coffee in the morning. Sometimes I catch myself looking toward the front door, half expecting him to come trotting inside with his favorite ball in his mouth.

People say time heals all wounds. I don't think that's true.

Thor came into my life as a fluffy Golden Retriever puppy, full of curiosity and joy. Like most Golden Retrievers, he loved everyone. He had an uncanny ability to make strangers smile. We'd walk through town or down the beach, and people couldn't help but stop to tell me how beautiful he was. They'd ask if they could pet him, and Thor never met a person he didn't think was a friend.

We lived just across the street from the dog beach in Ormond Beach, Florida, and he knew exactly where we were going every time we picked up his leash. He would practically lead me there, tail wagging the entire way.

He wasn't much of a swimmer, but he loved to wade into the surf just enough to cool his paws before racing back onto the sand. More than anything, he loved his tennis ball. It didn't matter where we were or what else was happeningâif he had his ball, life was good.

Looking back now, those ordinary days became the moments I cherish most.

Then, one morning, our lives changed forever.

I had worked for a neurologist for years. If anyone should have been prepared for something like that, I thought it would have been me, but nothing prepares you for watching it happen to someone you love.

From that day forward, epilepsy became part of our daily lives.

Our world revolved around medications, specialists, emergency hospitals, blood work, and carefully planned routines. Every dosage or missed meal mattered. Every subtle change in his behavior made me wonder if another seizure was coming.

I learned to recognize things most people would never noticeâa certain look in his eyes, a slight change in how he walked, moments when he seemed just a little different.

Hope became measured in days without a seizure.

Then another seizure would come, and we'd start over.

Most people saw the happy Golden Retriever. They saw the dog running down the beach, wagging his tail, carrying his ball. They didn't see the nights spent sleeping lightly because I was afraid I wouldn't hear him if he seized. They didn't see the medication schedules taped around my life or the emergency plans rehearsed in my head over and over again.

One morning stands out more than any other.

Thor wasn't a cuddler. As much as I wished he were, he usually preferred to sleep nearby rather than pressed against me. But that morning, he climbed into bed and lay back-to-back with me.

I woke up to him having a seizure beside me and rushed him to the emergency hospital.

I didn't know then that it was the beginning of the hardest chapter of our journey.

Epilepsy is cruel because it gives you hope just often enough that you believe tomorrow might be different.

We fought with everything we had for months, celebrating every seizure-free stretch, no matter how short, because when you love a dog with epilepsy, you learn to celebrate the smallest victories.

Despite everything he was carrying, Thor never stopped being Thor.

He still greeted people with excitement, still insisted on bringing me his ball.

He still looked at me with complete trust, as if I could fix anything.

That trust was both the greatest gift and the greatest responsibility I've ever known. As the months passed, one question kept finding its way into my thoughts:

What if something happened when I wasn't there?

What if he had a seizure while another family member was watching him?

His collar carried my phone number. His microchip could identify himâbut only if someone thought to take him to a veterinary clinic or shelter to have it scanned.

Thor couldnât tell a stranger that he had epilepsy. He couldnât explain which medications he took or where to find them, or which neurologist knew his case.

After months of fighting with incredible strength, Thor lost his battle with epilepsy.

Suddenly, my life was divided into 'before' and 'after.'

His toys were exactly where he'd left them.

It's realizing that the routines you built your life around disappeared overnight.

People asked me if I would get another dog, but what they didn't understand is that another dog could never replace Thor. Love doesn't work that way.

As the weeks turned into months, I found myself returning to the thoughts that had haunted me throughout Thor's illness. Some things are beyond our control, but maybe there was a way to make sure another family wouldn't have to worry that critical information would be unavailable during an emergency.

I wasnât looking to start a business or be known for inventing something. But grief has a remarkable way of asking you one impossible question:

For me, the answer became honoring the dog who had given me so much.

Everything I've built over the past year in creating Bark-ID: The Worldâs Smartest Dog Tag has been my way of making sure Thor's life continues to matter.

His legacy isn't a product; itâs the love that inspired it.

If you've ever loved a dog, you understand that they leave paw prints on more than your floors.

They leave them on your routines. Your memories. Your heart.

Thor taught me patience, resilience, and he taught me how fiercely we can love another living creature.

And in losing him, he taught me that grief and gratitude can exist together.

I still miss him every single day, and I probably always will. But when I think about Thor now, I try not to think about the day I lost him.

The tennis ball that never stayed clean for long and strangers who smiled because they met him.

The countless ordinary moments that, in hindsight, became extraordinary.

Some dogs make the world happier simply by being in it, and Thor was one of those dogs, and I was lucky enough to be his person.

If there's one thing I hope his story reminds people, it's that we never get enough time with the dogs we love.

So throw the ball one more time. Take the walk. Let them stop and sniff.

Take too many pictures. Sit with them a little longer.

Because one day, those ordinary moments become the memories you'll treasure most.

Thor gave me a lifetime of love in the months we had together, and if his story encourages even one person to cherish their dog a little more today, let that be his legacy.

After losing her beloved Golden Retriever, Thor, to epilepsy in 2025, she turned her grief into a mission to help other pet families be better prepared for emergencies. She lives with her Golden Retrievers in Ormond Beach, Florida, where she spends most of her happiest days at the dog beach. âThe Golden Retriever Who Changed My Lifeâ is her first published personal story.

#8005. 10 Foreign True Crime Documentaries To Scratch Two Itches At Once

Travel the world or curl up on the couch to watch true crime documentaries? Why not do both?

Travel the world or curl up on the couch to watch true crime documentaries? It’s the universal conundrum. On the one hand, the world is a big and beautiful place full of opportunities to eat delicious food and meet new people and wear hats you would never wear at home. On the other hand, there are true crime stories that need to be solved by you in your pajamas on the couch under a weighted blanket.

How do you scratch both of those itches? Well, you could travel the world seeking out true crimes to solve yourself, but that would get pricey and probably pretty dangerous. You don’t want to become the subject of your own true crime documentary, after all. Instead, settle in on a long, rainy weekend (or when it’s bright and sunny, I’m not judging) to watch these engrossing true crime documentaries set in beautiful locations around the world. It’s safer and the snacks are cheaper.

In 1996, French film producer Sophie Toscan du Plantier was found murdered outside her remote holiday cottage in the small village of Toormore. West Cork two days before Christmas. Sophie was just 39 years old and mom to son Pierre-Louis. A local journalist was one of the first to report her murder, and quickly became the main suspect. Netflix’s three-part docuseries Sophie - A Murder in West Cork covers not only Sophie’s tragic death, but also the struggle between Ireland and France to convict the killer.

Amy Lynn Bradley was just 23 years old when she went missing from the Royal Caribbean cruise ship Rhapsody of the Sea one early morning in March 1998. The ship was en route to the island of Curaçao. Her room showed no sign of a struggle, and several items were left behind. Authorities initially considered Bradley’s disappearance to be a potential accident or suicide, but Netflix’s 2025 three-part docuseries Amy Bradley is Missing speculates on several other possibilities that could have happened in the sunny tropics.

We do not love a scam artist. Especially one who preys on women looking for love, as Israeli conman Shimon Hayut aka Simon Leviev did between 2017 to 2019. Hayut swindled millions of dollars from women in the Netherlands, Norway, and other countries around Europe, leaving them destitute and broken-hearted. That’s the bad news. The good news is the way these women eventually found each other, banding together to bring Hayut to justice and try to reclaim their money. Netflix’s 2022 documentary The Tinder Swindler tells the story of three women who lost nearly everything to Hayut, and how they came together to bring him down.

The Netflix 2026 three-part docuseries Should I Marry a Murderer? will stay with you for a long time after the fact. Not just because it’s set in the gorgeous Scottish countryside, but because of the perspective it offers on what it might actually look like to find out the man you love is genuinely a murderer. Caroline Muirhead met handsome Scottish farmer Alexander “Sandy” McKellar on Tinder, and the two got engaged in 2020 after a whirlwind four month romance. When McKellar confessed to a murder that happened three years earlier, Muirhead stays with him. Told from her modern day perspective, Should I Marry a Murderer? Is an unflinching glimpse at what we might be willing to overlook in the name of love.

Vittorio Emanuele was nine years old when his family was exiled from Italy in 1946. His father was King Umberto II, and Vittorio was meant to be a prince until Italy voted to create a republic without the royal family. Living a life of luxurious exile, Vittorio was on the French island of Corsica in 1978 when he was involved in the death of 19-year-old German tourist Dirk Hamer. Netflix’s 2023 three-part series The King Who Never Was features interviews with Vittorio himself, as well as Dirk Hamer’s family members who were determined to see the privileged deposed royal charged with Dirk’s murder.

Michel Fourniret confessed to killing 11 women and one man in the picturesque Ardennes region of France between 1987 to 2003, making him one of the most notorious serial killers in modern French history. The Belgian killer only confessed after his seemingly submissive wife, Monique Olivier, provided police with enough information to force his hand. Which meant, of course, that she knew something of her husband’s crimes. More than police might have suspected, if the 2023 Netflix limited series Monique Olivier: Accessory to Evil proves anything. Olivier might have even been a willing participant in her husband’s horrific crimes. Chilling.

Fair warning for the 2019 five-part Netflix docuseries Who Killed Little Gregory? - the entire series revolves around the awful kidnapping and murder of 4-year-old Grégory Villemin in a small village in eastern France. Grégory’s murder has never been solved, and this docuseries delves into the disturbing allegations that members of his own extended family might have murdered the little boy. This one is equal parts difficult to watch and completely engrossing.

If you’re looking for some real-life Scandinavian noir to get you through the dark nights of fall, you’ll want to check out The Lørenskog Disappearance, Netflix’s five-part docuseries based on the true story of real life Norwegian billionaire Tom Hagan. Hagan’s wife Anne-Elisabeth Hagan went missing from the couple’s opulent home in October 2018, and a ransom note asking for nine million euros was left in her wake. The police originally believed Anne-Elisabeth was kidnapped, but began to suspect murder when the alleged kidnappers didn’t continue to reach out. While this 2022 limited series is a drama and not a straight documentary, it really delivers on Scandi vibes and billionaire intrigue.

British tourist Grace Millane was taking a gap year to travel the world when she ended up in New Zealand in 2018. She planned to head back home to her family for Christmas. She never made it back home. Millane was reported missing by her family, with police conducting a massive search in Auckland and the surrounding area before zeroing in on Jesse Kempson, her final Tinder date. The 2024 documentary The Lie: The Murder of Grace Millane on Amazon Prime, features interview tapes with Kempson as he is interrogated by police, and his subsequent attempt to use the so-called “rough sex murder” defense for killing the 22-year-old. On her birthday.

If you’ve been thinking of spending a bit of time in the UK along the coast, the Apple TV series Coastal Killers will either intrigue you or scare you off, depending on your perspective. Instead of focusing on just one true crime story, Coastal Killers has eight seasons of stories of mayhem in lovely little seaside towns in the UK...

...Which should keep you busy as you plan your next potential trip.

#8004. 4 new-school landline phones that help kids chat safely without screens

If your kid wants their first phone, these new options offer 90s nostalgia in spades.

By Audrey Goodson Kingo Updated Oct. 23, 2026

We independently select and share the products we love—and may receive a commission if you choose to buy.

If you fondly recall twirling the phone cord around your fingers while sharing the hottest 4th grade gossip, you can now give your kid the very same experience.

Fueled by Millennial nostalgia for our screen-free childhoods and concerns about online safety, parents are turning to a new-school twist on an old-school concept: the landline phone.

For kids who are craving connection to their classmates but may not be ready for access to the world wide web, these so-called ‘dumb phones’ are a pretty smart alternative.

That’s because smartphones and iPads can be a great way to chat with classmates, but they require a much higher degree of parental oversight. Not to mention, it’s a pain to pry a kid away from an iPad when their FaceTime call is complete.

The new batch of landline phones eliminate those concerns, since they are strictly for talking, and they work via WiFi, with a much lower monthly bill than a traditional landline connection. (And calls between models are free for some of the brands below.)

The 90s are back, baby, and so are the era’s iconic see-through phones, thanks to the latest limited-edition colorway from Tin Can. The company has almost cornered the market on smartphone alternatives, due to its clever concept: The phone’s design is an homage to the days when kids connected tin cans together via string to stay in touch. Nowadays, the phones connect via WiFi, and calls between cans, as they’re called, are free. (So are calls to emergency services.) For $9.99/month, your kid can call any number on an approved contact list. Just like on landlines of old, the cans come with speed dial, voicemail and speakerphone, and you can even set calling hours, so your social butterfly doesn’t chat all night.

The newest entrant on the market, Waffle Home phones are similar to Tin Cans, with a couple more features: The cord is removable, so your kid isn’t tethered to one spot to chat. (A plus or a minus depending on how much supervision you prefer!) Waffle Home phones also have caller ID, giving kids a heads-up before they answer. Similar to voicemail, kids can send voice notes when their friends aren’t free to talk. Like Tin Cans, calls to emergency services and between Waffles are free, but Waffle’s free plan also includes one non-Waffle connection (say, to your cell phone). Unlimited calling to non-Waffle numbers (including international calls to 50+ countries) is $9.99/month.

Ooma is a longstanding, publicly traded telecommunications provider, and its newly-released MyPhone is a great option for parents who want screen-free nostalgia paired with proven reliability. The phone looks exactly like the model every Millennial had growing up, and offers many of the same features as Tin Can and Waffle Home, but at a lower price point. (Calls between Ooma lines are free, and it’s only $7.99/month for a service plan that offers unlimited calls in North America.) Like the Tin Can and Waffle, parents can limit who can call, and kids can receive voicemail messages. There’s even a “party-line” feature for three-way calling when your kid’s gotta dish with more than one friend.

Pinwheel is known for its Android smartphone that offers built-in parental controls, so it’s no surprise the company also launched a landline model for parents who want to give their kids a phone with even fewer bells and whistles. The company’s Pinwheel Home Classic model is another chip-off-the-90s-block, a landline that connects via WiFi and is available at a lower cost than its competition. Calls to 911 and between Pinwheels are free, and the company offers two more calling plans up to $9.99/month for unlimited calls to any external number. As with the other options on our list, parents can manage who can call.

The DJ’s debut album, Come to Mommy, is a refusal to pick one version of herself, and a reminder that we don’t have to either.

Many parents fear that AI is taking over their teens’ ability to think for themselves. But with some open communication, you can raise kids that are aware of AI’s risks and rewards.

I thought I was giving my kids everything. Instead, I was missing the moments I worked so hard to create.

The season may be winding down but there’s plenty you can do now to protect those tubers so your dahlias come back stronger next summer. These 5 secrets unlock your best blooms ever

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

The first fall frosts bring a dramatic and abrupt curtain call to flower borders. And for any dahlias that might have been bursting with dinner-plate blooms just days earlier, it can come as a bit of a shock when freezing temperatures leave them limp and shriveled. For new dahlia growers, this sudden collapse can be devastating. Yet while the stems and leaves may be wilting and the flowers may be done, the tubers remain very much alive and capable of producing decades of future blooms.

So take heart, because you can enjoy those gorgeous displays again, as long as you take the right steps now. The days following first frosts are critical if these tubers are to push new growth out next year. These Mexican and Central American natives need care in order to see out the next few months. If these tubers are subjected to hard-frozen subsoil or waterlogged winter mud, they might easily rot and perish.

To keep your favorite cultivars thriving year after year, you need to decide how to overwinter dahlias, either by lifting the tubers for indoor storage or by applying the right protection and insulation in milder regions. The right approach depends on your regional hardiness zone, local soil drainage, and weather. While it might be a little daunting at first, getting your dahlias ready for winter is a relatively simple process. Whether you lift or leave in the ground, here’s how to prime your dahlias for winter.

Timing is key if you want your dahlia tubers to survive winter, and it’s vital to pay heed to your USDA hardiness zone to help your dahlia tubers to survive winter. Never dig your dahlias before the initial frost. That frost sends a biochemical signal through the plant, letting it know that the growing season has ended. In response, the plant channels its remaining energy down into the ground, plumping up the tubers in preparation for dormancy. So allowing the blackened stems to rest untouched for a week or so after this frost ensures the tubers reach peak maturity.

Your overwintering choices will depend on where you live. If you are in zones 6 and colder, it’s best to lift tubers every fall. Winter ground freezes in these latitudes can be lethal for unprotected tubers. Zone 7 gardens are borderline: lifting is still advised, but tubers in sandy, well-draining soil can survive beneath heavy insulation. In mild southern and coastal regions (zones 8-11), many dahlia varieties can remain safely in the ground, provided winter soil drains freely and the tubers have some protection.

You don’t have to remove the tubers right after the first frost. Let the foliage die back naturally. Any green foliage is still collecting energy to store in the tubers. You don’t want to disrupt that process prematurely. However, if you are in a very cold climate where the ground is going to freeze before the foliage has died, don’t wait. Keep an eye on the weather forecast to decide when to dig and lift your tubers. The goal is to let them mature without freezing them. In warmer climates, you have more flexibility.

Before you start, check the soil with a soil meter like the Raintrip 4-in-1 Soil Meter from Amazon. This will help you determine when the ground is nearing that freezing threshold ahead of lifting or mulching. Dahlia type and variety matter, too. Massive dinner plate varieties (such as Café au Lait) produce heavy tuber clumps that require longer drying times, whereas compact varieties (like the Gallery series) form tight root balls that dry quickly. Whichever area and variety you have, these steps will help you to ensure your dahlias return with a bang next summer…

Sign up for the Gardening Know How newsletter today and receive a free copy of our e-book "How to Grow Delicious Tomatoes".

The first step is to cut back stems and foliage. Once the foliage has blackened and you have allowed the root system a week to absorb its final starches, you’re ready. Using sharp bypass pruners, sever the main stalks down to 4-6 inches (10-15cm). If you are after a pair of bypass pruners, the Corona BP Dual Link Bypass Pruners from Amazon are perfect for slicing through the thick stalks in a single pass without crushing vital tissue.

Leaving short, sturdy stems is vital, as it gives you a safe gripping point for lifting the heavy tuber clusters and reduces pressure on delicate tuber necks. You can also use them to attach identifying labels. Just make sure that you cut the stalks just before lifting. Dahlia stalks are hollow, so if you cut stems down and leave them through days of heavy rain, water will pool around the tuber and trigger rot. Cut on a dry morning and plan to lift tubers the same day to keep water from causing problems.

Now, you’re ready to lift your tubers, but do it slowly and carefully. The tuberous roots and the narrow neck that connects them to the crown can break easily. If these necks snap, twist, or crack during digging, the tuber becomes useless. Use a garden fork to dig several inches around the plant. Get under the roots with the fork, inserting the tines 10-12 inches (25-30cm) away from the main stem. Rock the fork handle backward to loosen the soil, working in a full circle around the plant.

Gently lift the clump, using the shortened stems to help, but don’t yank hard on the stalk. Once lifted, gently shake away loose clods of earth. Inspect the roots, and snip away any soft, mushy, or damaged tubers. However, resist dividing the tubers now. Those cuts can leave them vulnerable to rot or infections in winter storage. You can add a little sulfur power such as Bonide Sulfur Plant Fungicide Dust from Walmart to stems to prevent storage rots. Alternatively, dust stem cuts with a little cinnamon.

Your tubers will need a little time to dry before being packed away. Place them upside down on slatted wooden trays, wire screens, or newspaper in a shaded, frost-free, well-ventilated space at 55-65°F (13-18°C). Let the clumps dry for 2-3 days until the skin feels dry and leathery. But don’t leave them so long that the tubers begin to wrinkle or shrivel.

Pack the dry tubers in breathable containers, such as cardboard boxes, wooden apple crates, or plastic storage totes with the lids cracked open. Nestle the tubers in a sterile, moisture-buffering medium, such as dry vermiculite, horticultural perlite, coarse wood shavings, or peat-free coir. You can buy Miracle-Gro Perlite from The Home Depot to help cushion dormant tubers while absorbing excess humidity to prevent winter mold. Make sure individual tubers do not touch.

Move your container into a dark, unheated room, such as a cellar, basement corner, or frost-free garage. Make sure it holds steady at 40-50°F (4-10°C). Stored tubers need a balance of moisture and dryness. Check on the tubers a few times over winter. If they are too moist, repack in drier material. If too dry, give them a light spritz of water.

If you are in zones 8-11 (or a sheltered microclimate in zone 7), you can overwinter your dahlia tubers in the ground. However, success depends on 3 factors: mild winters, excellent winter soil drainage, and insulation. Heavy clay soil that stays saturated in winter will rot tubers in the ground, regardless of ambient air warmth. Wait for the first frost to blacken the leaves, then cut the stalks down to 2-3 inches (5-8cm). Immediately cap the hollow stem ends with small inverted plastic cups, foil wraps, or a dab of horticultural wax to prevent rain from channeling into the crowns.

After cutting back dead stems, spread a generous 4-6-inch (10-15cm) blanket of loose, organic mulch over the surface. Try team favorite Back to the Roots Organic Premium Mulch from Amazon for a lush bark mulch that insulates from freeze-thaw cycles and suppresses weeds. You can also use clean agricultural straw or chopped dry leaves for protection against cold snaps, while helping to maintain healthy soil aeration.

Container-grown dahlias are vulnerable to freeze-thaw shocks. Left on an exposed patio, tubers can turn to ice in hours, while ceramic and terracotta planters are prone to cracking. It’s wise to move the container to a sheltered location for winter. Just be sure the soil will stay dry and the storage area won’t freeze. Once frost kills foliage, cut the stalks back to 4 inches (10cm), cease watering, and allow the potting mix to dry out. In colder regions, move the pot to an unheated garage, shed, or basement where temperatures are 35-45°F (2-7°C). If indoor space is unavailable in borderline zones, cluster containers tightly against a sheltered, south-facing foundation wall.

Wrap the containers in heavy layers of burlap or thermal bubble wrap, and mound loose straw over the top of the soil as a light mulch layer. Sta-Green Burlap Blankets from Lowe’s are a great breathable option for insulating grouped containers against winter winds and chills. Alternatively, you can lift and store tubers, just as with in-ground dahlias. Unpot the root ball, gently tease away the potting mix, and store the bare tubers in crates of vermiculite, just as you would for in-ground tubers.

Just because this season is over, that doesn’t mean you can’t enjoy your dahlias again. A little extra effort now allows you to enjoy these gorgeous blooms year after year. Caring for your dahlias after the first fall frosts doesn’t require special techniques or time-intensive labor. A half hour is all you need to cut back frost-nipped stalks, lever tuber clumps from the earth, and pack them into cozy quarters, or protect them if you leave them where they are. If you do tuck your tubers away this month, you just need to check in on them occasionally over winter Next year, your tubers will be in great shape and fully primed to deliver your most breathtaking blooms yet.

#8001. Pyometra: Signs, Causes, and Care (Vet Answer)

We just sent a welcome email your way with a quick overview of what to expect (including those vital recall alerts).

Your female dog is drinking more, panting, lethargic, and you know something just isnât right. Never ignore that feeling. You know your dog better than anyone else, and if you think something is wrong, it probably is. And if your dog hasnât been spayed, you could be seeing signs of pyometra: infection of the womb or uterus that can turn deadly if left untreated.

Any dog with a uterus can develop a uterine infection, and, although rare, even dogs that have had a laparoscopic or âkeyholeâ spay, where only the ovaries are removed, can be at risk of pyometra. So, what is pyometra? Read on to find out.

An infected uterus or womb, sometimes referred to in practice as a âpyoâ, is a relatively common condition affecting entire female dogs. It occurs most commonly in middle-aged to older dogs, but cases have been reported in dogs as young as 9 months.

In dogs, the uterus splits into two branches or âhornsâ that allow multiple fetuses to be carried on each side. Female dogs come into season or estrus around every six months once they reach sexual maturity. This is when she becomes fertile and receptive to mating. If she becomes pregnant, all being well, she will deliver a litter of puppies approximately 63 days later. Sometimes there can be a âphantomâ or âfalseâ pregnancy, also known as pseudopregnancy, where the fluctuating hormones surrounding estrus and mating prepare the dog for pregnancy, even when fertilization hasnât occurred.

Every time a dog goes through estrus, her cervix relaxes and opens, and the lining of the uterus thickens in preparation for mating and pregnancy. Ordinarily, the cervix helps prevent dirt, debris, and harmful bacteria from entering the uterus, so when the cervix is open, the risk of contamination and infection increases. If fluid and bacteria accumulate, infection can set in over the following 2-3 weeks, resulting in pyometra.

There are two types of pyometra: open and closed.

The more common and less dangerous of the two, an open pyometra occurs when there is infection in the uterus, but the cervix remains open. Dogs with an open pyometra are often diagnosed more easily because owners notice a foul-smelling discharge coming from the vulva, or that their dog becomes obsessed with licking her nether regions.

Because the pus can drain out of the uterus, an open pyometra tends to be less of a threat than one that is closed. However, an open pyometra can become closed, and vice versa.

A closed pyometra occurs when the cervix has shut, locking infection inside the body. It is a far more dangerous situation because the problem is not always immediately obvious, and, as the infection continues, pus fills and stretches the uterus. This can bring a risk of septicemia (infection of the bloodstream) and uterine rupture, both of which carry a high risk of mortality.

The signs of pyometra usually appear around 2-3 weeks after estrus. As mentioned above, dogs with an open pyometra may have a yellow, greenish, or brown discharge from the vulva which, if you get close enough to discover, smells pretty awful. However, dogs that are quite clean may lick up any discharge before you notice, so itâs important to be aware of the other signs of pyometra, which include:

With each season a dog experiences, her risk of uterine infection increases. At each estrus, the cervix opens, and the repeated thickening of the uterine wall reduces its ability to contract and expel fluid and contaminants. Dogs over 7 years old are typically at higher risk, but pyometra can affect even young dogs.

The most common bacteria involved in pyometra is Escherichia coli (E. coli), responsible for around 90% of cases, usually from fecal contamination.1 Obesity, recessed vulvas, chronic diarrhea, and thick coats that regularly become soiled increase the incidence of fecal contamination of the vagina and uterus, putting dogs at a much greater risk for pyometra.

Studies have also shown that diet can affect the growth of pathogenic E. coli and therefore influence pyometra risk.2

The use of synthetic hormones to prevent embryo implantation or induce abortion in the case of accidental mating, or to suppress or delay estrus, has also been found to increase the risk of pyometra.3

Your vet will diagnose pyometra based on a combination of the history, clinical signs, and examination. They will usually perform a brief abdominal ultrasound. Pyometra appears as fluid inside the uterine horns, visible on ultrasound as discrete black circles or tubes.

pyometra in dogs,ultrasound findings and diagnosis

They will also perform some bloodwork to check for signs of septicemia and assess kidney function, hydration status, and rule out any other underlying issues.

The fastest and most definitive treatment of pyometra is to perform an ovariohysterectomy â spay the dog.

The first step in treating pyometra is to start antibiotic therapy and intravenous fluids. Depending on the severity of the situation, your vet may recommend that your dog stay overnight on these treatments before proceeding with surgery, or they may want to go ahead right away.

Occasionally, mild cases of pyometra can be successfully managed using a combination of hormonal treatments and antibiotics. However, dogs that have had one episode of pyometra have a much higher chance of having another, which is why surgery is usually recommended. Once the ovaries and uterus have been removed, a dog can never get pyometra again.

The surgical removal of the ovaries and uterus will completely eliminate the risk of pyometra. Dogs that are spayed earlier in life also have a significantly lower risk of mammary cancer.

In the last decade, advice regarding the timing of spaying has changed, and most vets recommend waiting until after the first season to ensure she has reached sexual maturity. For small breeds, the first season might occur at around 6 months, while for large or giant breeds, the first season may not happen until they are at least 12-18 months old.

In a keyhole or laparoscopic spay, only the ovaries are removed (ovariectomy); the uterus is left behind. This has become a popular option due to the perceived reduction in pain, discomfort, and recovery time. However, when performed on young, healthy dogs, the most challenging part of a routine spay is trying to convince the patient to stay quiet and calm after surgery!

Theoretically, by removing the hormonal factor, ovariectomy should prevent pyometra. However, in the case of ovarian remnant syndrome, where fragments of ovarian tissue are left behind, uterine infection can occur.

Breeding from a dog that has (or has had) pyometra is not recommended. The circumstances that allow pyometra to form â open cervix, thickened uterine walls, contamination â can also make pregnancy riskier for the dog.

Additionally, pyometra can damage the uterine lining, reducing fertility and increasing pregnancy risks.

Before surgical spaying became common practice, allowing dogs to mate and have litters was likely seen as the best way to avoid pyometra. This is probably where the old wivesâ tale that âyou should let your dog have puppiesâ originated. These days, with millions of unwanted puppies in need of homes, and surgical sterilization being a relatively safe routine procedure, there is no longer any real justification behind the idea that dogs should have a litter.

If you think your dog might have a pyometra, do not delay treatment â the longer you wait, the worse things will get. If you are worried about costs, reach out to local charities or speak to your veterinarian â there may be payment plans or charitable funds available to help.

A dog is never too old to get a pyometra, so even if your dog is considered elderly, unless they have health conditions that make surgery or anesthesia too much of a risk, itâs far better to have them spayed when theyâre healthy rather than risk them getting a pyometra in old age.

Pyometra is a relatively common â and entirely preventable â disease in female dogs. Infection of the uterus can make your dog incredibly sick, and if left untreated, can even be fatal. Signs of pyometra usually appear 2-3 weeks after a season and include increased thirst & urination, lethargy, inappetence, fever, discomfort, and, in the case of an open pyometra, vaginal discharge.

If you suspect your dog may have pyometra, contact your vet immediately â do not delay.

If your dog hasnât been spayed, talk to your vet. Remember, prevention is always better than cure.

#8000. Thinking About Adopting A Cat? Here Are 4 Things To Ask Before Bringing Them Home

Catster is reader-supported. When you buy via links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission at no cost to you. Learn more.

This article was created in sponsorship with Mars, which helps make content like this possible.

Pet ownership is booming, but when it comes to adoption, the biggest hurdle isnât willingness; itâs receiving the right support and guidance to adopt with confidence.

Despite there being more than one billion pets worldwide, with cat ownership specifically on the rise, new research from Mars found that 58% of pet owners have not adopted a pet from a shelter or rescue organization. Worries about the unknown, from a petâs health and behavioral history to understanding their nutritional and everyday needs, are just some of the factors that can hold people back from taking that next step.

For prospective cat owners, however, the right preparation and support can make all the difference, especially when nearly a third of respondents globally would consider it with the right support. Mars is #ClearingThePath to pet adoption by giving prospective pet parents practical, expert-backed guidance to navigate the questions that can arise before and after bringing a pet home.

Find out what medical care and health checks the shelter provides as standard. Some initial questions could be what veterinary care your cat has received (if any), including any parasite treatment, which vaccinations they have had, if they are microchipped or neutered, and whether they have any known health concerns or ongoing medications.

Once your cat is home, contact your local veterinarian to establish care for your cat. A check-up soon after adoption can help build a clearer picture of their overall health and create a plan for future preventative care. Itâs a good idea to arrange pet insurance as soon as youâve decided to adopt your cat so theyâre covered for any injuries or illnesses that may arise.

But health is only one part of understanding what your new cat needs to thrive. The SHINEâ¢ framework, developed by the Waltham Petcare Science Institute, looks at five interconnected areas of a petâs wellbeing: socialisation, health, individuality, nutrition and environment.

With that bigger picture in mind, ask the shelter about your catâs personality, temperament, energy levels, previous experiences and interactions with people, children or other pets. Understanding as much as you can about these different needs can help you consider how well your home, family, and daily routine will suit the individual cat, and how you can best support them once they come home.

Mars Research found that 71% of adopters change their petâs diet soon after adoption, but changing food immediately is not usually recommended unless a veterinarian advises it.

Ask the shelter what your cat is currently eating, how often they are fed, and whether they have any special dietary requirements. Your catâs food should be complete and balanced for their life stage, whether they are a kitten, adult, or senior. Keeping their food and feeding routine consistent initially can help make the move feel less disruptive.

If you want to change their food, wait a week or so to allow them to adjust, then do so gradually by adding a small proportion of the new food to their regular diet. On the first day, their old food should make up around three-quarters of the meal, with the new food making up the rest. Gradually increase the proportion of new food each day over a week, giving their digestive system time to get used to the new food.

If you decide to adopt a senior cat (7+ years),â¯diets designed for mature catsâ¯account for the burning of fewer calories throughout the day as well as increased palatability tailored to mature cat preferences.

Importantly, cats need diets that provide appropriate protein and essential nutrients, along with constant access to fresh water. Portion size, nutrition, and feeding style should reflect your catâs activity, age, body condition, and health; treats should remain below 10% of daily calories.

A veterinarian can help choose the most suitable diet if your cat has medical or weight concerns.

Although it can be tempting to let your new feline friend explore everywhere straight away, for many cats, a smaller and more predictable environment can feel much safer.

Consider keeping your new cat in one room before slowly giving them access to the rest of the home. During the first few days, keep windows secured and doors closed, and make sure they have everything they need close by.

Cats will seek out hiding spaces when they feel stressed, so itâs important to provide some quiet resting places while they settle in. Providing safe places to retreat to will help them navigate the unfamiliar sights, sounds, and smells around them.

Something as simple as a cardboard box placed on its side or an open cat carrier can offer a reassuring place to hide, giving them confidence to explore and interact.

Many pets need time to adjust to being alone in a new home. Start by gradually introducing short periods of separation and pairing alone time with positive experiences, such as treats, toys, or enrichment activities. Keeping departures and arrivals calm and predictable can also help build confidence and reduce stress.

If your pet shows signs of significant separation anxiety, such as destructive behavior, excessive vocalization, or distress when left alone, speak with your veterinarian or a qualified behavior professional for support and guidance.

From preparing for those first few days to supporting your petâs long-term health and nutritional wellbeing, the Mars Adoption Hub brings together trusted resources, practical advice and specialist tools designed to help you feel informed, supported and confident at every stage of the adoption journey.

Dr. Martin Whiting, BVetMed, BSc, MA, DipECAWBM (AWSEL), PhD, PGCert Vet Ed, FHEA, FRSB, FRCVS

Martin Whiting is a board-certified specialist veterinarian with a PhD in veterinary law and a master's in medical ethics. He has taught and published in these fields both nationally and internationally.

His career began in general and specialist practice before he joined the Royal Veterinary College as its first faculty member in Veterinary Ethics and Law. He moved to the Civil Service as Director of Operations within Home Office Science and Security, focusing on the regulation of animal research in the UK, and later became Director of Education at CVS Group Plc., overseeing their new graduate programme and establishing a new veterinary nursing school.

As the Global Head of Ethics and Welfare at Mars Inc., he is engaged in all facets of animal welfare, from veterinary care and responsible pet ownership to ingredient supply chain and ensuring research ethics are held to the highest standard.
